b2-nominalization.title: Verbal Noun: -(i)sh
b2-nominalization.explanation: Adding -ish (or just -sh after a vowel) to a verb stem turns the action itself into an abstract noun that can be the subject or object of a sentence: kitob o'qish foydali (reading books is useful), sport bilan shug'ullanish sog'liqqa yaxshi (exercising is good for health).
b2-nominalization.fact: This same -ish is what dictionaries strip away to list a verb's bare stem -- o'qish ("reading") and o'qimoq ("to read", the citation form) share one root, just packaged for two different grammatical jobs: one as a noun, one as an infinitive label.

dialogue.en: In your opinion, is learning a foreign language difficult?

b2-purpose.title: Purpose: -ish uchun
b2-purpose.explanation: The verbal noun in -ish combines with uchun ("for/because of") to express purpose: pul topish uchun ishlayman (I work in order to earn money), imtihonga tayyorlanish uchun kutubxonaga bordim (I went to the library in order to prepare for the exam).
b2-purpose.fact: Uchun on its own is simply the word for "for" used with any noun (sen uchun, "for you") -- purpose clauses in Uzbek are built by feeding it a verbal noun instead of an ordinary one, not by inventing a separate "in order to" word the way English did.

dialogue.en: Why do you run every day?
I run in order to be healthy.

b2-wonder.title: Wondering: -mikan
b2-wonder.explanation: -mikan (from -mi, the question particle, plus ekan, "apparently/it seems") expresses genuine uncertainty or wondering, closer to "I wonder if..." than a direct question: u keladimikan? (I wonder if he/she will come?).
b2-wonder.fact: Because -mikan is built from the same -mi used for ordinary yes/no questions, it can be tacked onto almost any statement to soften it into a musing rather than a real question directed at a listener -- a way of thinking out loud grammatically.

dialogue.en: I wonder if the weather will be good tomorrow.

b2-probability.title: Probability: -sa kerak
b2-probability.explanation: Kerak, already familiar from obligation ("must go"), also expresses probability when attached after a -sa form: u uyda bo'lsa kerak (he/she is probably at home) -- a guess based on evidence, not a requirement.
b2-probability.fact: The exact same word kerak covers both "you must" and "it must be [the case]" -- English needs two different senses of "must" for this too, but Uzbek marks the difference structurally: obligation uses a plain infinitive before kerak, probability uses the conditional -sa form.

dialogue.en: He/she is probably stuck on the way.

b2-relative-case.title: Participle + Case in Chained Clauses
b2-relative-case.explanation: A -gan/-digan participle clause can itself take a case ending once it modifies a noun that is then further marked: men o'qigan maktabning direktori (the principal of the school where I studied) -- the whole clause "the school where I studied" gets the genitive -ning before direktori attaches.
b2-relative-case.fact: This is how Uzbek builds what English needs a full relative clause plus a possessive for ("the principal OF the school WHERE I studied") out of a single chain of suffixes on ordinary nouns and participles, with no relative pronoun ("where", "which") anywhere in the sentence at all.

dialogue.en: Where is the company where you worked located?
It's located in the center of Tashkent.
